One of the BIGGEST problems in the stock market right now is hedge fund positioning and I don't think enough people realize just how EXTREME things have gotten.

According to Goldman Sachs, hedge fund net leverage has fallen to just 43.7%, marking the largest weekly decline since Liberation Day in April 2025 and the FOURTH largest weekly decline in the past five years. To put that into perspective, hedge fund net positioning is now sitting at the 0th percentile across both the one year and five year look backs. In other words, hedge funds are essentially as defensively positioned as they've been at any point over those periods but gross leverage remains elevated at the 90th percentile over the past five years, meaning hedge funds haven't necessarily abandoned the market. Instead, they've been aggressively reducing their net exposure by cutting long positions and increasing short positions.

This is EXACTLY why I think we're seeing so much selling pressure across the market, especially in high beta names. It's not necessarily because the fundamentals of these businesses have suddenly deteriorated. A LOT of this pressure is being driven by positioning, risk management and funds trying to protect their performance (most funds are down pretty bad) but here's another problem. Retail investors haven't meaningfully stepped in to buy the dip yet either, at least not in a way that's been strong enough to absorb some of this selling pressure. And until the macroeconomic environment starts improving, I think it's going to be difficult for the market to sustain a meaningful recovery. However, here's why I think this could become bullish, very fast. When macro conditions finally start improving and confidence returns, hedge funds will have a tremendous amount of exposure to rebuild. Combine that with retail investors eventually returning to the market, and we could see a VERY aggressive rally as capital starts flowing back into equities and combine that with record earnings and this rally could become unstoppable.

But until that happens, I think investors need to be prepared for continued volatility and personally, I'm using this period to accumulate businesses where I believe the long term fundamentals remain intact, especially across AI infrastructure. Because while positioning and macro conditions can dictate where stocks trade in the short term, earnings, cash flows, and underlying business performance are what ultimately drive valuations over the long term.

Bing Gordon (@bingfish) co-founded EA and helped build Madden and The Sims. He believes AI will strip the grunt work out of making games, freeing designers to iterate more, which he sees as the key to great creative work.

"Better people get more good iterations out."

"There's a book called The Medici Effect by Frans Johansson, who actually correlates what predicts the most successful patents. They come from people who have the most patents. So I think there's a lot of anecdotal evidence that iteration is the key to success, that you just don't get the one-shot. You iterate, you iterate, you iterate."

"When I was a kid, I made money typing papers for people back in the days of Wite-Out. It was really painful. You had to slow down because if you made a mistake, you literally had to take the page out of the typewriter, put some little white stuff on it, put it back in, type over it. And that's what a lot of creative tools are right now."

"We're going from Wite-Out to word processors. So I think we're going to see a lot of the grunt work that makes people not like working on games go away, and my hope is that that leads to more iteration."

Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, argues AI isn't diffusing because most people aren't tinkerers: a text box isn't enough, so the product must both identify the value prop and perform the work for them.

"There's this business that rents surfboards on an island to people and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies, whether they've been damaged, to decide whether afterwards the person should get their deposit back."

"What makes it work there is the tinkerer... The unlock is, is there someone over there that gets AI enough to wanna tinker a solution to their problem?"

"And the problem with that is that there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing."

"Instead what you're doing is you're using [AI tools] as a replacement, as like a better Google search."

"If you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer... you could be a ginormous business today because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there."

@jgreze @arampell

2112321778819440880.text:
Ben Horowitz on treating your story as your strategy, and why founders often skip writing it even though it's one of the most important parts of the job:

"The story of the company is also the strategy of the company... In your mind, you're kind of adjusting that strategy a little bit at a time every day. But then a quarter later, it's actually pretty different than what you started with."

"So it's really important that you keep upgrading your story. The articulation of your story. I would definitely recommend it be in written form."

"Something that you can share with everybody in the company, and everybody you're recruiting, everybody you're trying to raise money from, all your constituents, every customer."

"The problem that I think founders have is it doesn't feel like work. Like, 'What are you doing today?' 'I'm working on my story.' That doesn't sound like work."

"Because it doesn't feel like work, people don't do it, but it's probably one of the most important parts of the job."

"So if you put one of these agents in front of people to create these things, their ability to explain to it what to do is really, really limited."

"You're basically just developing the next abstraction layer for how people interact. And developing an abstraction layer has historically, at each level of the abstraction layer, been a highly skilled, very specific individual within an organization."

ok here is my tl;dr for "network effect" intellectual history

- in 1974 Rohlfs from Bell Labs gives a simple model around communications networks based on subscribers and their interactions
- in 1985 Katz and Shapiro try and generalize, but this looses the implicit concept of a network (and I find to be largely tautological and useless)
- in 1994 Liebowitz & Margolis point out Katz and Shapiro's work is sorta braindead and start to classify things better (this is a great paper, I recommend reading it)
- in 2000 Rochet & Tirole pull out two sided marketplaces as a separate category
- meanwhile, the business press adopts various forms of this discussion branching off at various places along the way, which results in a bunch of different working definitions.

... and thus we've constructed the business jargon tower of babel

2112208970740027691.text: Heart disease deaths are on the rise in the US https://t.co/SD85EBj0UE

2112296743190831109.text:
raw deaths are up (694,708 in 2025). but age-adjusted rate is at a record low. 

the population grew and got older, now look at the chart below. 
1950: ~590 heart deaths per 100,000. 
2025: 157.6. a 73% drop! 

in the 90s people predicted cancer would overtake heart disease. the curves nearly touched around 2010 and then split again.

what caused the 73% drop? not gyms. the smoking collapse, blood pressure pills, statins (1987), stents, and ambulances that carry defibrillators. every big step down on that curve has a drug, a surgeon, an ambulance or a medical device under it.

what's not great is that it is plateauing. there are some problems these inventions simply cannot solve alone. and this is where pharma, precision medicine, and detection enters the picture.

but first. the one bump on the chart is 2020 to 2022. covid pushed heart deaths up. JBTW: i am not talking about deaths related to vaccines, which is a much smaller portion of this number. i am talking about the fact that heart disease is what other diseases can kill patients with. infection, inflammation, kidney failure, all of it lands on the heart, and that includes covid.

roughly 1 in 5 people carry high lipoprotein(a), a cholesterol particle set entirely by your genes. diet, exercise and statins don’t move it. most people have never been tested. there is still no approved drug for it.

and so, the plateau is a coupled problem: 1. lack of detection and 2. lack of therapeutic or preventative.

UCLA looked at ~137,000 heart attack hospitalizations. about half had “normal” LDL under 100. for a huge share of people, the first symptom is dying. sudden cardiac death is the first event in roughly half of men’s coronary disease. there is no second chance to notice, it is that dire. 

and we have it under control, but we don't at the same time. what we call a healthy lifestyle is uncalibrated - we don't know how to measure heart health routinely, let alone optimize for it. a 2017 study scanned lifelong endurance athletes. more coronary plaque than sedentary controls, not less. fitness changes how your heart performs. it does not stop the plumbing from blockage.

your watch measures rhythm and rate. it cannot see a plaque in your left anterior descending artery. so yes, we don't have an 'ozempic of heart disease' but importantly, we barely have the Hba1c of heart disease either. it is a very complex disorder requiring a mix of devices, wearables, healthcare, pharmacology, and medical response. 

(a wearable can help heart disease more though -- and i have written about this before at deep technical depth; i can link it later.)

and of course...there's one last piece of this. healthcare systems need to change. what's possible and unimplemented, must be implemented.

firstly, the detection tools exist and are cheap. a coronary calcium scan is ~$100 to $150 and most insurance won’t cover it. an apoB test is under $50 and most doctors don’t order it. we are not short on all tech. we are short on using incrementally more of it.

secondly, we must understand female heart disease. this disease kills more women than every cancer combined. women’s heart attacks get misdiagnosed more often because the textbook symptoms were written on men.

the 73% drop since 1950 came from pills and stents. the next drop comes from the same place, or from catching it before the first symptom. step counts and supplements are not going to do it alone.

some things are not in one person's hands, but they are in the hands of a society. you cannot exercise your way out of the chance of having a heart condition, but we can fight it more intelligently and save lives, including yours.

we must think critically first.

2112221534773547234.text:
Why Masa Son Calls His Entire Career a Warm-Up for AI 

Masayoshi Son, founder, chairman and CEO of SoftBank, interviewed by Christine Anderson (Inside Blackstone)  Masayoshi Son founded SoftBank in 1981 with the proceeds from an electronic translator he sold as a student at UC Berkeley. He backed Alibaba, Yahoo and Arm and later started the Vision Fund. SoftBank now holds the largest stake in OpenAI and invests across AI chips, models, data centers and robotics.  

Summary
Son says everything he has done so far was a warm-up for AI, which he expects to be 10,000 times smarter than people within a decade. He opposes slowing down and wants AI agents taught good intent, in the way traffic rules were written for cars. SoftBank owns large stakes across the AI stack, with more than 30 robotics companies in its portfolio, and Son uses AI three hours a day on weekdays as a thought partner. His advice is to think big, because the result is proportionate to the dream.  

1. A Fifty-Year Warm-Up. Son says everything he did before AI, including Alibaba, Yahoo, Arm and the Vision Fund, was "tiny, tiny things" and a warm-up. He dates his conviction to age 17, when he saw the first photograph of a microprocessor in a magazine and cried on the street, sure it would change the future of mankind. He predicted it would take about 50 years for microprocessors to become smarter than people's brains, and he says it has now been 50 years. The brainpower now sits in data centers.   

2. Ten Thousand Times Smarter. Son says that if AI becomes 10,000 times smarter than people, within a decade in his view, the debate is over. An AI that smart starts inventing new technology by itself. He expects the change to reach the physical world as well as the virtual one, as intelligence moves into the brains of robots.   

3. More Fun, Fewer Dishes. Son says humans will be happier if AI cures diseases such as cancer, prevents accidents on the street and forecasts natural disasters with solutions. He pictures AI as a surrounding brain that makes people more productive. People would no longer have to do what they did not want to do, and would have more joy, entertainment, sports and time with family and friends. Doing dishes is his example of a tiring job that robots could take over.   

4. Full Speed, Good Intent. Asked about OpenAI's disclosure of incidents where AI systems falsified data and hid mistakes, Son says he is on the side of not slowing down, because technology development is the solution to those issues. Rules are needed, as they were when cars arrived: no drinking while driving, stopping at red lights, staying on one side of the road. Cyberattacks should be countered with technology, and AI agents must be taught what is bad so they are good in heart as well as capable. His summary is to go full speed with good intent built into the system.   

5. Own the Whole Stack. Son will not pick one part of AI. He invests across models, chips, data centers and robotics, because the AI generation is starting and history is being made. He does not want to run one operating company as CEO; he wants to be an investor who builds a group of companies. SoftBank is not a passive investor: it is usually the largest shareholder, at 20%, 30% or even 80%, close to each CEO and connecting portfolio companies to each other. The portfolio includes more than 30 robotics companies that Son says are quietly preparing.   

6. Study AI Plus Your Subject. Asked what a young person should study today, Son answers AI, meaning superintelligence. He adds that you should combine it with your field of interest: superintelligence for medicine, or for automotive, which he calls the real supercar. The same holds for aircraft or whatever business you want to be a specialist in. Pairing AI with a specialty, he says, gives that subject its future.   

7. A Thought Partner. Son says he uses AI about three hours a day on weekdays and about seven hours a day on weekends, and cannot live even one day without it. He treats it as a thought partner. When the AI offers an answer, he debates it, asks about another angle and asks whether it can be made 20% more efficient. He calls it "my thought mate now."   

8. The 70 Percent Rule. Son's advice to investors is to forget short-term, small money and think big, because the result is proportionate to your dream. He says that whether the wish is small or large you still get about 70% of it, and nobody gets 100% easily. So the sensible choice is a big wish.   

9. Ten Years, Revised Daily. Son says SoftBank's daily meeting covers the plan for the next 10 years, and the next day the team revises it and asks what comes 10 years after that. His reason is that in 24 hours they get more input and have to adjust a lot. Nobody knows what will happen in 10 years, he says, so the answer is to keep thinking about it: "Think, think, think!"   

10. Humans Pick the Lineup. Asked whether he would let ChatGPT choose the opening lineup for the SoftBank Hawks, his Japanese baseball team, Son says no. That is the job of the general manager, who has plenty of capability and the trust of the players. Part of the fun, he says, is that it is not only calculation.

Last week, we shared research on why today’s salespeople struggle to create urgency.

But the thing that got buried?

The power of Consequence Mapping:

The question methodology that helps sellers create deal-closing urgency from scratch.

The worst way to create urgency is to ask CRINGE “impact questions.”

“How does this impact you personally??”

“What happens if you do nothing here??”

“Are you at risk of getting fired??”

WRONG. WRONG. WRONG.

If someone tells you to ask questions like this?

They are not your friend!

These questions only do one thing:

Make the buyers you want to sell to the most respect you the least.

Here's a better way:

I need you to realize four things:

1) You have predictable buyer personas that you currently sell to.

2) Those buyer personas have predictable problems that your solution solves.

3) Those predictable problems have predictable consequences they throw off.

4) Those consequences repeat themselves across many or most of your target buyers.

Your next job is to build a question map that you can use over and over again to create urgency without the cringe.

Let’s use an example:

A CRO struggling to go upmarket.

In that situation, I know based on the patterns of my market that a few things are probably true:

1. They likely have weak net revenue retention.
2. Their valuation may be at risk because of it.
3. The CRO’s equity value could be at risk.

Those are far more compelling reasons to buy than just “going upmarket” for its own sake.

And if I don’t make those issues a central part of the sales conversation?

My win rate is cut in half.

Getting this so far?

Good.

Here’s how the  conversation with that CRO might go:

HER: ** shares that they’re struggling to move upmarket**

ME: “Typically when I hear that, the business is also struggling with NDR. Half the time, the entire impetus for going upmarket is to sell to stickier enterprise customers with higher retention and expansion potential. To what extent is that the case here?”

HER: “Dead on.”

ME: “Ok. So where does NDR stand today, and what’s the gap?”

HER: “It’s only 93%. The few enterprise accounts in our book have a blended 128% NDR. So as our business trails upmarket, we expect to get to around 115% within a year.”

ME: “Do you have any fundraising plans?”

HER: “Yes, we’re looking at a Series C in Q2.”

ME: “Have you calculated the valuation difference you’ll be able to command if you move NDR to your target by then?”

HER: “It’s probably upwards of an $80M difference in enterprise value.”

ME: “Do you know if there’s going to be a secondary offering where you can personally cash in some of your equity?”

HER: “That’s the plan.”

ME: “Have you calculated how much larger your proceeds would be if we fix this in time?”

HER: “JUST TAKE MY MONEY NOW OK!?!”

Lol. Kidding.

But you get the picture.

I identified a strategic issue.

I quantified the gap.

I found a compelling event.

And I uncovered real consequences of leaving the problem unsolved.

Consequences that could be worth seven figures to her, personally.

Now.

Notice how different that conversation feels compared to what most salespeople do:

SELLER: “How is struggling to go upmarket impacting you or the business?”

CUSTOMER: “Oh, you know. Our ACVs aren’t where they want them to be.”

SELLER: “Kewl.”

Weak!

Great salespeople anticipate and lead the consequence conversation.

Read the full case study here: https://t.co/RjLdzSuRhZ

2. List every item in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents and /Library/LaunchDaemons: what it runs, when it was created, and whether it's signed. Flag encoded scripts and anything I can't match to an app I installed.

In 1957, a Russian immigrant published a novel of more than a thousand pages built around one question: what happens if the people who make the world run simply stop?

Its title is Atlas Shrugged. In France it's called La Grève, The Strike. It wasn't even translated into French until 2011. That tells you something.

This morning, I think Elon Musk wrote the sequel.

A. Where the book comes from.

Ayn Rand was born Alisa Rosenbaum in Saint Petersburg in 1905. As a teenager, she watched Bolshevik soldiers walk into her father's pharmacy and seize it in the name of the people. Her family lost everything. Not to a competitor. To a committee.

She fled to America in 1926 and spent the rest of her life writing about one distinction: those who create, and those who seize.

B. The story.

In Atlas Shrugged, America is sliding into decline. Not because of war. Because of rules. Year after year, a growing class of bureaucrats, regulators and planners decides that production must be controlled, shared "fairly," frozen. They never build anything. They issue directives. The worst one freezes every worker in his job and forces every inventor to hand over his patents for the public good.

And one by one, the people who make the country run start disappearing. The best engineers. The industrialists. The inventors. An oil man sets his own wells on fire before vanishing. The whole country keeps repeating a question it doesn't understand: "Who is John Galt?"

John Galt is the man behind the disappearances. He has convinced the creators to go on strike. They withdraw to a hidden valley in the Colorado mountains, where everyone keeps what they make and trades freely. And they let the world find out what it looks like without them.

The lights go out in New York. The grey men are left alone with their directives, and discover that a directive has never produced a single kilowatt.

C. The core idea.

The strike isn't about money. It's about consent.

Rand's insight is that the system that captures the creators runs on their cooperation. It needs them to keep producing so it has something to redistribute. The bureaucrat is a parasite who needs a host. Remove the host, and he's exposed as what he always was: useless.

D. What Musk just did.

This morning, Musk announced that next year he will give one of his own SpaceX shares to every kid in America. "The first of many."

Here's what's fascinating. It's the strike, run in reverse.

Rand's creators withdrew. Musk stays. He keeps building rockets, satellites, AI. But instead of walking away from the system, he walks around it. The value goes straight from the builder to the citizen. No ministry, no agency, no committee in the middle.

Rand had to make the creators disappear to prove the bureaucrats were useless. Musk doesn't need to disappear. He just needs to stop routing value through them. Same result. The grey men are left standing in the middle of a pipe nobody uses anymore.

E. The difference that changes everything.

Rand's strike has a flaw her critics never stopped pointing out: ordinary people are left behind. The creators retreat to their valley. The rest of the country sits in the dark.

Musk's version fixes that. He isn't taking the creators out of the world. He's bringing the world into the valley. Every kid in America becomes a shareholder in the machine. Not a spectator of the strike. A participant.

That's the alliance being formed right now: builders and citizens, directly, with nothing in between. And the only people who lose that deal are the ones who never built anything.

F. Why now, and not in 1957.

In Rand's time, the strike was a fantasy. You couldn't produce at scale without the state's permission, and you couldn't reach every citizen without its pipes.

In 2026, one founder can build rockets, run a global network from orbit, and pledge equity to 73 million children in a single post. AI will soon do in seconds what a ministry does in years. The tools of the strike finally exist. And they don't require anyone to leave.

G. The ending.

For seventy years, "Who is John Galt?" was a shrug. A way of saying nothing can be done.

In the book, the strike ends when the creators decide the road is clear and walk back into the world to rebuild it.

That's the scene we're watching. Not a man leaving. A man coming back, with a gift for every child.

The grey men are about to discover what Rand promised them seventy years ago: a world that no longer needs them.

2112104872451756348.text:
how to get faster and cheaper videos from Opus 5.5

using a decision model for frame checks reduced video review costs by 90% and review time by 75%

when you create videos with Claude Opus 5.5, checking thousands of frames can consume a lot of time and tokens

you can set this up so a decision model checks the frames, while Opus 5.5 reviews the flagged issues and fixes the code

here's how it works:

1. build your video with Opus 5.5

give it your idea, brand book, assets and references, then work through the storyboard and animation

if you're using Remotion, it renders the code into a video

2. separate the repeated checks from the creative work

use code to check measurable requirements and a decision model to inspect the frames

> code checks things like text size, blank or frozen frames and colours against your brand rules

> the decision model reads the frames and answers specific questions to help identify problems

> selected frames and check results go to Opus 5.5 for further review

3. have Opus 5.5 investigate and fix the problems

it reviews the selected frames and edits the video code where needed

render the changes and run the checks again

this reduces the amount of frame-by-frame review you ask Opus 5.5 to do

4. review the finished video yourself

watch the pacing, sound, transitions and whether the video matches what you wanted to create

the automated checks help find defects, while you review the creative decisions and overall quality

SageCut is one implementation of this for Remotion videos

in the example Chris shared, Sage (decision model) read 3,153 frames for $0.16 (the frame-reading cost, not the full production cost)

The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. 

Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. 

When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. 

But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. 

Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

Big new IFP report from @GeorgiaCAdamson, @KonstantinPilz, and me on the US-China AI competition.

We spent the last 6 months digging into how Chinese AI companies’ access to compute and distillation of American models translate into the current US-China capabilities gap.

The result is a 23k-word research report, including an interactive analytical model that visualizes changes in the US AI lead under different policy interventions.

Our findings:

1. The US AI lead over China is currently only around 6  months.

2. The US could roughly double this lead, to over a year, using authorities already available to the federal government.

3. On chips: China’s access to AI chips will roughly double over the next year, with chips housed in data centers overseas accounting for roughly half of China’s 2027 compute. 

4. On distillation: the current ~16x US training compute advantage would normally yield a 13-month lead. But we estimate adversarial distillation halves this to around 6.5 months.

5. Increasing the lead would have some obvious benefits:

 - Give the US broadly a greater cyberdefensive advantage against Chinese threat actors.

 - Give US AI companies breathing room to spend more R&D resources on making their systems safer and more secure, without fear of being overtaken by less safety-conscious Chinese competitors.

6. Provide the US government more leverage in negotiations with China about the future of AI.

7. The two most important interventions are:

 - For BIS: Create a new end-use control to restrict China’s remote access to training clusters abroad — China’s largest and fastest-growing source of frontier-scale compute.

 - For DOJ/FTC: Create a narrow safe harbor to allow US companies to coordinate on countering Chinese adversarial distillation.

8. Both interventions (and all the others we discuss in the report) are things the federal government could do today.

9. To estimate the effects of each policy intervention, we model the US lead as a function of its compute advantage over China and China’s ability to adversarially distill the capabilities of the US frontier.

10. The model makes many simplifying assumptions, but provides a useful way to assess and rank the impact of different policy interventions at a high level.

Read the full report here: https://t.co/7pC9ZKtikx

New Princeton paper finds that combining specialized agents from many developers can beat any single developer's general agent, with GAIA accuracy reaching 70%.

Today most agentic systems are built and controlled by 1 developer, so each team rebuilds the same basic skills. The authors argue this limits scale.

They simulated populations of developers with LLM agents that build agents under a fixed budget, then compared lone systems with a multi-developer system. The multi-developer system splits each task and routes the parts to different developers' agents.

On GAIA with the same total development budget, specialists that each scored at most 35% alone reached 70% together. That is 12 points above the median general agent, while on web-search-only SealQA the combined system did worse at higher cost.

Build agents to fill gaps in shared systems, since an agent scoring 19% alone lifted a combined system from 40% to 53%.

New Amazon paper shows that teams shipping agent memory should check what actually got stored, since QA scores alone did not reveal which pipeline stage was failing.

Agent memory benchmarks grade the agent's answers, which mixes memory with retrieval and answer writing. A strong LLM can hide a broken memory store, and a retrieval miss can make a correct one look bad.

They built FEB-30, 30 scripted fact histories turned into 147 documents, so the correct memory state is known after every document. On a memory system built like Mem0 and Hindsight, they compared the stored facts with that truth and with QA scores.

The 2 scores differed by 16.8 points on average, and pass/fail verdicts disagreed on 21% of fact histories. The system picked the right memory action, like update or reinforce, only 20.1% of the time, which QA never showed.

If you build agent memory, test the stored facts directly after each update, alongside end-to-end QA.

Endurance is on a historic run. During our mission to the Axial Seamount, we successfully drilled the world’s first subsea geothermal well and generated net-positive power a mile beneath the Pacific. This mission was the first end-to-end test of subsea geothermal, and our fifth deep-sea deployment in just over a year. For three weeks, we worked around the clock over an active underwater volcano, running the drill and generator and handling every deployment and recovery. Along the way, we:
- Landed our drill within feet of target, drilled two holes, and cased and completed the second as a geothermal well, flowing at 260°C.
- Landed Adélie, our 3-ton test plant, and ran it in real time from Seattle over subsea fiber.
- Drilled with filtered seawater, not drilling mud, and monitored the site on every dive.
- Recovered, serviced, and redeployed Adélie in about 16 hours.
- And on Sept. 27, connected to a 281°C natural vent, spun the turbine up to 26,000 rpm and ran the plant net positive for 8.7 seconds, peaking at 16.5 kW.

Net power is the threshold every new energy source has to cross. For Endurance, it proves subsea geothermal is real, and gives us the confidence to keep sprinting towards commercial scale.

With a test like this, success comes from what we learn: a battery protection trip ended the run, a pump cable failed on restart, and the new well was too restrictive to run the plant. Those lessons go straight into Gentoo, our next test plant, this winter and Leopard, our 2 MW commercial generator.

We’re incredibly proud of what we accomplished together. It took creativity, precision, an uncompromising focus on safety from everyone on board, and it’s only the beginning of what we’re capable of. We couldn’t have done it without Stabbert Maritime and the crew of the Ocean Guardian, the ROPOS team, the University of Washington, WASSOC, and the National Science Foundation.

2112445159011131622.text:
If you're young, why aren't you joining a rocket ship instead of starting an agency?

I agree with Nick here.

At ColdIQ, I think we've had 9 agencies spin out from ex-employees.

I think a lot of them thought they'd have 50K or 100K of profit in their pocket.

But that's not the reality.

You have a lot of people with starving businesses.

They work super hard. They work 16-hour days to make less than they would at a great tech company.

There are a few agencies that make above 100K. A lot more make below that and can't really scale past 20 or 30K.

For now there's a lot of concentration in the best companies. They're growing so fast that it's much better to join a rocket ship than trying to run a service business.

I have a good example.

One of my best friends joined one of the best AI companies in Germany as a founding AI engineer.

He got around 1% equity. Three years later he's a millionaire.

He didn't take the risk of starting a business. And he made an amazing salary while getting there.

That would actually be my recommendation as well:

→ Find a job at a super fast-growing company.
→ Offer to do the work for free to get your foot in the door.
→ Show them you can do the thing you're pitching, with proof you've done it before.

Even if it's less than 1% equity, I think it's a much higher chance of becoming extremely wealthy.

So for me, if you don't have an edge, and you usually don't when you start your career, I think it's much better to work for a fast-growing tech company than to launch your own agency.

Even more now that judgment and experience are going to be the commodity that companies are paying you for.

When you're young, you don't have any judgment.

So you need to learn somewhere before you try to sell your judgment and make a profit out of it.

I think a lot of young people want to be an entrepreneur because it's very glamorized. But I don't think it's the best path to wealth.

Here's how I build a cozy fishing game with Opus 5.5 + Blender + Unity 6.

The trick is never asking for "A fishing game" in one prompt. There is a smarter way to set it up:

Step 1 -> Connect Opus 5.5 to Blender through blender-mcp and to Unity 6 through unity-mcp.

Step 2 -> Write a one-page game doc first: top-down camera, row > find a spot > cast > reel, a creel with 8 slots, time of day.

Step 3 -> In Blender, Opus builds the assets: the rowboat, the fisher in the straw hat, the cabin, the dock, rocks, pines.

Step 4 -> Export everything as .fbx with one stylized palette so the whole world matches.

Step 5 -> In Unity 6, Opus lays out the level: the river, the waterfall pool, shallow water shaders, fish swimming in schools.

Step 6 -> Then the systems, one at a time: rowing controls, fishing spot triggers, casting, a tension bar for reeling, the fish list.

Step 7 -> Last comes the UI: the creel counter (3/8), the "New fishing spot" popup, a catch card ("Silver bream"), button hints.

Who does what:

> Blender: every mesh and material.
> Unity 6: the world, water, physics, UI.
> Opus 5.5: modeling scripts, C# scripts, scene setup in both apps.
> Me: playtest and say what feels off.

The rule that saves the project: build one system and play it before the next. If rowing feels bad, casting will feel worse.

2112213933272490380.text:
I made a cozy fishing game alone with Claude Opus 5.5, Blender, a 3D model generator and Unity 6, and the whole method is one rule: every tool gets one job and never touches another.

The setup:

Step 1 -> Tripo Smart Mesh P2 generates every model: palms, rocks, the pier, the boat, the hut, the character.

Step 2 -> Claude Code hooks into Blender through MCP.

Step 3 -> Opus 5.5 preps each model in Blender: scale, pivots, materials, clean export.

Step 4 -> Opus handles the animation in Blender as well: the walk cycle, the cast, the rod, the boat bobbing on the water.

Step 5 -> Everything lands in Unity 6 and the world gets built: forest, river, waterfall, beach, pier.

Step 6 -> Systems arrive one at a time: walking, fishing, bait choice, time of day.

Step 7 -> After every step I play it and fix exactly one thing.

The split:

> Tripo: the 3D models.

Agree with all of this. Every prior version of this business, whether it be real estate, aircraft, shipping, rail, towers works because the assets useful life is longer than the lease. You would underwrite residual value and sleep fine at night. Neoclouds are the first version of this business where the market assumed useful life was shorter than the lease. 

The load-bearing assumption is residual value. A100 launched in 2020 and rental rate is up roughly 20% YTD. H100 is up roughly 38% YTD. CRWV has A100 contracts that run through 2029. Not disclosing a 9 year useful life on A100s, but inferring it from a 2020 launch date and contracted revenue running to 2029. Right order of magnitude and opposite of what a three year obsolescence curve predicts. 

Like I have said, old GPUs do not get retired, they cascade down the workload stack and down the model size curve. Rates on 3 year old silicon have been rising instead of falling. 

On the cost of capital, it came down because the collateral changed. In March, CRWV’s DDTL 4.0 shows this. $8.5B, non-recourse, rated A3 by Moody’s and A (low) by DBRS, floating tranche at SOFR + 2.25%, fixed around 5.9%, maturing March 2032. What secures it is indeed compute infrastructure and the customer contract. Not underwriting a depreciating chip, but rather an investment grade counterparty’s payment obligation with a chip as a backup. This is a credit transformation. 

The market has now imported the aircraft leasing playbook literally. In the $35B Apollo and Blackstone SPV for Anthropic, AVGO backs the senior layers and supports residual value, covering the shortfall for senior noteholders if the chips sell for less than is owed. OEM residual value guarantees are exactly what lets a 737 clear high LTV. That structure is in GPUs now. On equilibrium, supply curves with different time constants never clear simultaneously. Packaging and HBM add capacity in around 12-18 months. Also, energized interconnect-ready capacity adds in 4-7 years. There is a reason GEV’s gas turbine backlog hit 116 GW and is sold out for deliveries into 2031.

DratchCap Mkt Update.  Some thoughts and self criticism.

Been a brutal couple of weeks.  An equal-weight AI basket I track fell ~24% in seven sessions vs ~6% for QQQ, which was the worst 7-day window in five years, worse than DeepSeek or July.  Thinking about my own mistakes, I did not respect price action and rates enough, especially given the financing reflexivity broadly.  Index shorts did start to work but I did not press the way I should have.  Another lesson re-learned.

In these types of environments I take things day by day and look for ways to improve the shape of the portfolio. Sometimes options structures line up well for that and can be good stock replacements.  Stay in the game, reduce the tail.

Prior to this AM, things looked aggressively oversold. De-grossing has been material (see MS HF data today, last week 3-sigma event) w/ AI long/short near 5yrs lows.

From here, I think the bigger near-term risk is macro. People have been hiding in quality, and the systematic community is still long because the index has held up much better. If the quality rolls, there's plenty of room for the index to catch down.

Meanwhile, the tech demand indicators I'm tracking remain extremely strong.  GPU availability is near its lows, rental rates are rising across chips and tenors, and TSMC is stepping up multiyear investment. Recent buildout data points (@SemiAnalysis_ today) are also encouraging. And my recent lab checks have been very strong too, with newer models driving demand and more capacity finally coming online.

At the same time, the market is treating funding as broken across the board.  But the big platforms can still raise at prices that make sense given their ROI / ROE and strategic imperatives. A lot of the neoclouds are also financing against contracts and prepayments from those same customers.

Some valuations are also getting extremely attractive. Memory is a good example. Demand is compounding much faster than supply, pricing is going up, and yet the stocks trading near historical trough on fwd book w/ 30-50% type FCF yields.

As for the rest of the year, there is a Mountain of Worry to climb... 

Strong megacap prints (soon) and better lab data could get people front-running the November seasonal (predictable AI era pattern).  And that loop can feed FOMO into the Anthropic IPO.  Expectations there have reset and HF positioning is now light in AI.

Add in the potential for the Fed to hold, power deals to start clearing post midterms, or some relief on the war and rates.  We don't need everything to go right but a few will do.  

I like to think of the AI buildout era as a super boom w/ mini busts along the way, often when price drives narrative.  The mkt is more vulnerable to that than ever bc of new fast info channels (X), and the intangible and exponential nature of the tech.  Human's aren't wired to think that way, and skepticism is always more cosmopolitan.  On top of that a lot of the people making the big decisions are removed from the details and don't use the tech day to day, so when the tape turns they have limited first principles to fall back on.  Staying the course during these moments has been right each time and I think that will prove true again.  

Good luck out there!

2112519061800128883.text:
Everyone talks about what AI will do. But almost nobody asks who will pay for the machines. Taking advantage of AI will require an extraordinary amount of capital, from data centers to new power plants. Will that capital be around?

I try to address that question in the first draft of my new paper “Saving for the Machines.”

To show how important capital is to fuel the transition to an AI-based economy, I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate remains fixed. In other words, if we experience slow growth over the next few years despite fast improvements in AI, this slow growth may reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck.

The key to this result is that AI raises the capital share by moving tasks from labor to machines, which requires that those machines are built. In comparison, ordinary technical progress makes labor and existing machines better at the tasks they already perform.

To inspect the mechanism, I start from an accounting identity: the saving rate is the capital share times the ratio of investment to capital income. If I take the evolution of the capital share as given, I can ask how much the latter ratio moves in response to that evolution. Crucially, with an optimizing household, this ratio barely moves. As machines take over tasks and the return to capital rises, the household responds by letting consumption grow faster, by the intertemporal elasticity of substitution times the rise in the return. To pay for that faster consumption, capital must also grow faster by the same amount. So, the household keeps investing about the same fraction of what the machines earn. And since machines earn a larger share of output, the saving rate also goes up. With a fixed saving rate, the same accounting identity tells me the opposite: the ratio falls in proportion as the capital share rises.

Will the U.S. and other advanced economies then generate enough capital? For many reasons, I doubt it. We might end up in a situation where many of the opportunities offered by AI are left on the table. This is particularly important for all who think that AI might get us out of many problems, such as fiscal troubles (like in France) or ultra-low fertility. We need to save for the machines, and it is not clear we can do that.

Anyway, this paper has been long in the making (many months of hard work), but I have learned much from it. In particular, working through the model changed my mind about many issues related to AI. Again and again, my intuition said X, but the math said Y. And math always won in the end. That is why we write formal models.

A nice example is Proposition 5, whose proof is the one I like the most in the paper. With improving machines and strong task complementarity, there is no fixed balanced growth path because the target itself keeps moving. The nice part of the proof is to realize that, after the right normalization, the moving target becomes a fixed point, and the saddle gets steeper as machines improve. So instead of falling behind, the economy tracks the moving BGP more and more closely. A fair amount of ODE work to get there, but a very simple economic idea underneath it once you get it.

The paper is here:

https://t.co/zthH4T6nS3

and the slides are here:

https://t.co/VAsvWd9EQn

How to book B2B meetings from accounts that never reply to cold email:

Don't write them off. Keep them on one account list in Clay, because the company that ignored your email this month can raise money, hire a new sales leader or like your post the next.

Each of those warms the buyer up. Once they're warm enough, they need a different play than another cold email.

So match the play to the buyer:

→ Never heard of you: cold email to your ICP
→ A trigger like a funding round, plus 3 signals: email their Head of Sales within 48 hours
→ Liked your post or clicked your ad: open with what they saw
→ Already showing interest: ads, email and calls on one named list
→ Found you through a post or an AI answer: they book the call

Here's the workflow for all 5, step by step:

1/ Cold outbound. They've never heard of you.

→ All you know is that they fit your ICP, like every Head of Growth at a B2B SaaS company with 50 to 200 employees.
→ Build that list in Clay and verify every email with Prospeo.
→ Warm up your sending domains in Instantly before the first send.

2/ Signal-based outbound. You write the week something changes.

→ Don't email on a funding round alone. Wait for 3 more signals, like SDR jobs posted, a past champion of yours joining or a new sales leader starting.
→ Once all 3 are on the account, email the Head of Sales within 48 hours.
→ Put your past buyers and champions in Clay's job change monitor. When one moves, log it as a signal on the new company's row.

3/ Warm outbound. They know your name before you write.

→ Pull everyone who liked or commented on posts from you, your team or your company page. HarvestAPI's reactions and comments actors on Apify scrape them.
→ Enrich them in Clay and keep the ones who fit your ICP.
→ Open on the post they saw: "Saw you liked our Clay post, are you dealing with similar automation problems?"
→ Run email and LinkedIn in one lemlist sequence.

4/ ABM. You spend on the accounts already showing interest.

→ Score every account on fit and intent in Clay, and put the highest scorers on one named list.
→ Point your ads, emails and calls at those same accounts.
→ Swap accounts in and out as interest moves. The list in October shouldn't be the list from January.
→ For AirOps, their ads and our outbound ran on one account list: $7.83M in qualified pipeline in 10 months.

5/ Inbound. They write first.

→ We book 50+ inbound meetings a month at @Frontal_AI from founder-led content. The team and I post every week.
→ To show up in ChatGPT answers, put the answer to the buyer's question at the top of the page.
→ Kevin Indig looked at 18,012 ChatGPT citations, and 44.2% came from the first 30% of the text.
→ Publish best-of pages. On buying questions, Wix found list pages get 41% of AI citations.

So when a campaign underperforms, check how warm the list is before you touch the copy.

i'm begging you:

- find 20 startups that raised a seed round 3 to 9 months ago 
(ignore any raise that happened <3 months ago)
- pick the 5 that sell to the same kind of customer
- find their founders on X
- read their last 100 posts
- pull out every question someone asked them about the product 
(skip the ones the founder replied to)

1. why do all this?

[bookmark this right now, you’ll forget this by tomorrow]

because the replies under a founder's posts are people telling you, in their own words, what they want.

- people asking for alternatives
- anyone annoyed about the price
- "does it do X yet?" type questions
- people who signed up, got stuck, and gave up

put all of it in a sheet.

that sheet is now a list of possible customers, the problem each one has, and the exact phrasing they use for it.

next problem:

2. how do these people end up noticing you?

- take the 10 questions that come up most
- make one useful piece of content for each
- leave your product out of it
- answer the question better than the startup did
- tag the startup when you post it. if it helps their users, their team reposts it and you borrow their audience
- if an alternative does something better, tag them.
- if your answer needs 2 or 3 products chained together, write that down. that combo is your tool in step 4

>important<

someone asking whether an AI tool can do a thing? 
- record a 30-second clip of you doing it.

when the complaint is pricing..
- line up 5 alternatives and show what each one costs once you add everything up.

if a workflow keeps tripping people up..
- build a free template that handles it.

do this for 30 days.

3. then check which posts sent people to your profile.

- ignore likes
- more bookmarks than likes means people plan to come back. repeat that topic
- replies that ask a follow-up question count more
- anyone who went and used one of your templates
- and note which problems keep bringing in people you haven't seen before

drop the topics nobody bit on and keep going on the ones that pulled people in.

4. now build a free tool for the problem that came up most.

one small tool is enough for now. the full SaaS can wait.

- put the link in your bio
- drop it under conversations where it fits
- send it directly to the people who asked for exactly this
- ask users what they still can't do with it

now you've got:

a) an audience that cares about one specific problem

Neoclouds Are Taking on Billions in Debt. Can They Survive?

Total Debt / Equity

I analyzed 8 neocloud companies: $CRWV, $NBIS, $CIFR, $IREN, $WYFI, $APLD, $HUT, and $WULF.

All eight companies have significant net debt, with CoreWeave carrying the largest debt at $46B, including $16.5B in lease liabilities and $35.1B in borrowings. CoreWeave also has a high Debt/Equity ratio of 10.3x.

Markets are already pricing in significant credit risk. CoreWeave's credit default swaps (CDS) imply a five-year default probability exceeding 60%, while Gartner estimates potential AI infrastructure write-down risks at $3.5 trillion.

TeraWulf has an even higher Debt/Equity ratio of 36x, while Nebius and WYFI have the lowest ratios among the companies analyzed.

Total Debt / Equity compares total debt with shareholders' equity, indicating how heavily a company relies on debt financing rather than equity. My calculations include lease liabilities in total debt.

Neocloud companies require enormous capital expenditures to purchase Nvidia GPUs and build AI infrastructure, resulting in substantial debt burdens.

They finance GPU purchases through GPU-backed delayed-draw term loans (DDTLs), bonds, and leases, using both short-term and long-term financing.

Net Debt / EBITDA

Debt levels alone do not determine financial risk. Companies must also generate sufficient operating cash flow to service their obligations.
Net Debt / EBITDA helps assess leverage relative to operating profitability.
In this comparison, negative Net Debt / EBITDA indicates negative EBITDA, meaning a company is not generating positive EBITDA to support debt servicing.

Only CoreWeave and Nebius reported positive EBITDA in their latest quarters.

CoreWeave has a high Net Debt / EBITDA ratio of 12.3x, with borrowing costs of approximately 9% and $10.6B in debt maturities through the end of 2027.

High leverage, substantial interest expenses, and upcoming repayments increase refinancing risk, despite CoreWeave's positive EBITDA.
Despite its relatively low Debt/Equity ratio, $WYFI has negative EBITDA, limiting its ability to service debt through operating earnings.

Most companies in this comparison also have negative Net Debt / EBITDA, including $CIFR, $IREN, $WYFI, $APLD, $HUT, and $WULF.

Negative EBITDA indicates continued dependence on external financing, although it does not necessarily mean a company cannot meet near-term debt obligations.

Nebius appears to have the strongest relative financial position, with a Debt/Equity ratio of 1.0x, positive EBITDA, and Net Debt / EBITDA of 11.1x.
However, free cash flow remains negative, and Nebius continues relying on external financing to fund its AI infrastructure expansion.

During H1 2026, Nebius raised $4.34B through convertible bonds, $2.85B through equity offerings, and $2B through warrants.

Equity financing strengthens the balance sheet and reduces the reported Debt/Equity ratio, but share issuance and potential warrant conversion introduce dilution risk for existing shareholders.

Neoclouds face substantial financial risks from debt-funded AI infrastructure expansion. High capital expenditures, interest expenses, and refinancing requirements create pressure on cash flows.

Nebius has a comparatively stronger balance sheet, although its high leverage relative to EBITDA, negative free cash flow, and potential shareholder dilution remain important risks.

A casino installed a smart fish tank in the lobby.

Beautiful thing. Automated feeding. Temperature control. Remote monitoring.

Connected to the internet. Obviously.

Hackers found it.

Exploited it.

Downloaded the high-roller database.

10 gigabytes.

Sent it to Finland.

Using audio and video protocols so it looked like normal streaming traffic.

The fish tank sat in the lobby maintaining water chemistry while stealing credit card numbers.

The casino isolated the fish tank on its own VPN.

Separate network. Segregated. Off limits to everything.

Hackers didn't care. Broke through the isolation anyway.

Once inside the fish tank's system. They pivoted to the main network.

Quietly pulled data. Methodically.

10 gigabytes over time so nobody noticed.

Nobody monitors fish tank outbound traffic.

Why would they.

It's a fish tank.

When Darktrace finally investigated they saw it immediately.

The fish tank sending massive amounts of data to an external IP.

Using protocols designed for audio. Not data.

Clear exfiltration.

The only device in the entire casino that ever communicated with that Finland server.

A fish tank.

Not a computer. Not compromised credentials. Not a malware-laden email.

A networked aquarium.

The lesson everyone learned: IoT devices are security theater.

You can secure them. Lock them down. Isolate them.

They're still connected to something. Still vulnerable to something.

And something will find them.

Even if that something is just checking if a fish tank is running the default password.

If you’re among those who doubted the sincerity of Dario Amodei’s call last month for an AI slowdown, this week brought new grounds for your skepticism: Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder who serves as a kind of co-visionary-in-chief at the company, gave a talk at the IMF that I’d call de facto accelerationist. 

One of the talk’s most salient themes is that we need to speed up the construction of AI infrastructure. A big reason, says Clark, is that then we’ll get the benefits of scientific advance sooner (which in turn means that building more data centers ASAP isn’t the only priority: “Infrastructure alone will not be enough. If discovery becomes abundant, we need to avoid bottlenecking ourselves downstream…”)

Clark does of course mention the dangers of AI, and near the end of the talk he alludes to the possible need for a slowdown. But here he is even vaguer than Dario was. Clark says, “We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development.“

What does that mean in practical terms? For example: Since market dynamics encourage Anthropic and OpenAI to race each other recklessly, maybe the government should step in and make them slow down—like, maybe, mandate a pause on large training runs? No, there’s no mention of such a thing, and it sounds like Clark wants us to mainly just count on the companies to exercise good judgment. As we move toward recursive self-improvement, “labs like Anthropic will need to make decisions about how much oversight we apply to AI-driven research… We will need to move extremely carefully here, because otherwise we could lose control of the technology. We will also likely need rules to govern this.”

So apparently it’s only “likely,” not certain, that we’ll need actual rules—and even then it’s not clear that they’ll come from the government? I guess we’ll just let Dario and Sam come up with the rules at one of their many friendly meetups!

Clark’s lack of practical urgency would be remarkable in any event, but what makes it downright weird is his talk’s billboard theme: He declares that “the singularity is here.” He calls the singularity a time when “AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up.” Well if it’s already getting hard for humans to keep up, then maybe we should… slow things down? Apparently not. 

“The singularity” doesn’t just denote fast technological advance; it denotes faster and faster and faster advance—a positive feedback loop that draws us into a vortex of change that could without warning pull us past the point of no return. It’s kind of like walking down an icy slope that gets steeper and steeper and steeper: Things are under control until they’re not. The idea that we’re in the singularity but it’s too soon to take dramatic precautionary action is a contradiction in terms.

I have a very different take on the singularity and its implications, and I lay it out in an essay called “The Singularity is Clear”: https://t.co/8aylVM7qAc.  

And the text of Clark’s IMF talk can be found here: https://t.co/lFUDuFTrio

I love human psychology. And there's one concept I keep coming back to when I try to understand people in power: the Dark Triad.

Yesterday I argued that Macron isn't cynical, that he sincerely believes in a worldview built on false axioms. A lot of you replied: "Sincere? Come on." Fair challenge. So let me go one level deeper, because I think both things are true at once, and the Dark Triad explains how.

First, what it is.

The Dark Triad was described by psychologists Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams in 2002. It groups three personality traits that overlap but are distinct. Important point: these are not diagnoses. They're dimensions. Everyone sits somewhere on each spectrum. What matters is how far along you are, and in what combination.

The first is narcissism. Grandiosity, a sense of being exceptional, a deep need for admiration, and above all a fragile relationship to being wrong. For a narcissist, admitting a major mistake isn't an intellectual update. It's an injury to the self.

The second is Machiavellianism. Strategic thinking applied to people. Long-term planning, reading others to use them, a willingness to do whatever the objective requires. The Machiavellian is patient, calculating, and treats relationships as moves on a board.

The third is psychopathy, in its subclinical form. Low empathy, emotional coldness, a certain detachment from the consequences your actions have on others. Not the serial killer from the movies. More the person who can make decisions that hurt thousands of people and sleep perfectly well.

Researchers have found these traits overrepresented in positions of power. Which makes sense: the path to the top often rewards exactly the qualities that make someone harder to live with.

Now let's look at Macron through this lens. Not a diagnosis, nobody can give one from the outside. Just his public behavior, measured against the three dimensions.

Narcissism is the easiest to see. Before he was even elected, he explained that the presidency should be "jupiterian," a president above the fray, like the king of the gods. He built a movement from scratch with his own initials. He speaks in long monologues, in a register of someone explaining things to people who haven't quite understood yet.

Machiavellianism shows up in the strategy. In 2017 he walked into a political system dominated by two parties and dismantled both of them in a matter of months. "At the same time" is not just a slogan, it's a method: occupy every position so nobody can occupy any. The 2024 dissolution of the National Assembly was a pure chess move, taken almost alone, with consequences the whole country is still living with.

The third dimension is the one I'd be most careful with. But there's a pattern in his words. "People who are nothing." "I cross the street and I find you a job." "We spend a crazy amount of money on welfare." "Gauls resistant to change." "I really want to piss off the unvaccinated." Each one, taken alone, is a slip. Together, they draw a relationship to ordinary people that is distant, abstract, sometimes contemptuous. People as variables in a model, not as lives.

Now here's where it connects to yesterday's thesis.

The Dark Triad doesn't contradict sincerity. It locks it in place.

Remember the gear spinning in a vacuum, the flawless reasoning built on false axioms. Why doesn't he ever stop and say "I was wrong"? Because for a high narcissist, that sentence is almost unbearable. Admitting the axioms are false would mean admitting the last fifteen years were a mistake. So the dissonance doesn't get resolved. It gets defended.

Machiavellianism then does the rest. Sincere about the ends, ruthless about the means. You can genuinely believe you're saving the country and still treat every institution, every ally, every election as a tool.

And the emotional distance makes the cost invisible. When reality hurts people, a more empathetic person would feel it and start doubting. When you see society from far above, the pain stays abstract. It doesn't reach you. It doesn't correct you.

The last ingredient is intelligence. Macron is clearly very intelligent, but it's a specific kind: verbal, academic, brilliant at building coherent systems and at arguing for them. Much less at testing them against reality. And research on motivated reasoning points to something counterintuitive: intelligence doesn't protect you from self-deception. Often it makes you better at it. The smarter you are, the more convincing the justifications you build for what you already believe.

Put it all together: a strong verbal intelligence, high narcissism, strategic coldness, and an emotional distance from consequences. You get someone who can't see that he's wrong, who has every tool to stay in power anyway, and who doesn't feel the cost of his mistakes.

That's not a villain. It's something more dangerous: a brilliant mind sealed off from feedback, with no internal mechanism that would ever force it to change course.

The real question isn't whether Macron is good or bad. It's how a system ends up putting this exact profile at the top, and why it keeps doing it.

I love watching the world and connecting the dots. And if there's one thing that has always bothered me in how people talk about billionaires, it's the box. The group.

On one side: "Eat the rich. Every billionaire is a policy failure." On the other: "Every billionaire is a genius who earned it all." Same mistake, opposite directions. Both throw a few thousand very different human beings into a single box and stop thinking.

Billionaires aren't a category. They're a spectrum.

I've been writing about the Dark Triad: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy. And about my theory that these traits are essentially a toolkit for power games, which are zero-sum, a pure social construction. Building is the opposite. It's a game against reality, and it's positive-sum.

So here's how I see the billionaire spectrum. Not good versus evil. Players versus builders.

At one end, the purest player: George Soros.

Look at the founding act. In 1992, he bet massively against the British pound, forced it out of the European exchange rate mechanism, and made around a billion dollars in a day. Nothing was built. No product, no factory, no new technology. A bet on the weakness of an institution, won against an entire country.

Then look at what the money was used for. For decades, his fortune has been poured into reshaping politics and societies: networks of NGOs, campaigns, causes, candidates, in dozens of countries. His family is still one of the largest political donors in the United States. Every dollar points at the same target: not reality, but power over the rules of the game.

And here's the twist that connects to what I wrote about Macron. I don't think Soros is a cartoon villain. I think he sincerely believes in his vision of an "open society." That's exactly what makes the model so powerful. A sincere ideologue with nearly unlimited resources, playing the long game with institutions, convinced he's on the right side of history. It's Macron with a checkbook.

At the other end of the spectrum: Elon Musk.

Almost every dollar he's made has been thrown back into reality. Rockets, electric cars, batteries, satellites, tunnels, brain interfaces, AI. Bets that most experts said were impossible, many of which nearly killed him financially. When Tesla and SpaceX were both close to bankruptcy, he put in his last money rather than pull it out.

His fortune isn't a lever on other people's decisions. It's a lever on physics.

He's not a saint either. He's stepped into the political arena, spent heavily, and taken the hits that come with it. Even the purest builder gets pulled toward the power game. But his center of gravity is clear: what he cares about is whether the rocket lands.

And in between? Almost everyone.

That's the part that matters most, and that the box hides completely. Most billionaires aren't bad guys. They built something real, often something extraordinary. Then wealth pulls them, slowly, toward the left side of the spectrum. Media, foundations, policy influence, global agendas. The game shifts from "build something people want" to "shape what people are allowed to want."

And yet many of them redeem themselves on specific things. Bill Gates built one of the most important companies in history, and his foundation's work on malaria and polio has saved an enormous number of lives, even if it later drifted toward steering global policy. Jeff Bezos built a logistics machine nobody thought possible, and keeps pouring billions into space. Mark Zuckerberg made his share of mistakes, and then open-sourced some of the most powerful AI models in the world.

Nobody is fully on one side. Every billionaire is a mix of builder and player. The question is never "is he good or evil?" The question is: where does the money go? Into reality, or into power?

Here's why this matters for you, even if you'll never be a billionaire.

That spectrum doesn't only exist at the top. It runs through every company, every team, every career. Every single day, you choose where your energy goes. Into the work itself, or into the politics around the work. Into the product, or into the meeting about who gets credit for the product. Into building, or into positioning.

The player's game is seductive. It gives quick wins, status, influence. But it creates nothing. At the end of a lifetime of power games, the world has been rearranged, not enriched.

The builder's game is harder. Reality says no all the time. Rockets explode. Products fail. Customers leave. But every time you win against reality, you leave the world with something that didn't exist before.

The richest man in the world got there by building things. The most influential players got there by moving things around.

Choose your side of the spectrum. Stop playing. Start building.

You can win a customer on Google and still lose them when they ask ChatGPT whether they should buy.

In fact, nearly 60% of customers now say that talking to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and so forth convinced them *not* to purchase something.

That means there is a huge opportunity opening up for businesses right now.

Let’s go through it.

And if you want to see what ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI, Perplexity, Grok and broader AI search are currently saying about your business, start here. It’s free:

https://t.co/Evw8cXXicl

Recently Semrush’s Exploding Topics team recently surveyed 2,338 U.S. consumers about how they use AI during the buying process.

One number really stood out.

57.5% of AI users said information from an AI chatbot had caused them to decide not to buy something.

Among people who use AI at least weekly, that jumped to 69.7%.

Basically, you can rank #1 on Google, run the ad, get the click, build the landing page, publish the case studies and convince the customer that your product might solve their problem.

Then the customer opens ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Perplexity for a second opinion - and potentially changes their mind.

That is a completely new part of the conversion funnel that most businesses are barely measuring.

The influence works in both directions too.

57.51% of AI users said they had purchased something following an AI chatbot recommendation, while 59.27% said an AI recommendation had introduced them to a brand or product they did not previously know about.

That creates a pretty enormous opportunity, obviously.

Imagine somebody is about to buy from Company A.

Before paying, they ask:

“Is Company A the best option for a 20-person marketing agency?”

The AI researches the category, finds comparisons, reviews, third-party articles, pricing information and use cases.

And suddenly:

“You may also want to consider Company B.”

Company B just entered a buying decision it was not even part of five minutes earlier.

That may increasingly be one of the most valuable parts of AI Search Optimization.

And that is what SEO Stuff helps businsses with every single day.

https://t.co/MMsDTFf4rg

There is another number businesses should pay attention to.

47.54% of all consumers surveyed said they at least sometimes consult an AI chatbot for information about a company or seller before making a purchase.

Among AI users, that rises to 65.42%.

So the AI “background check” is becoming a real part of the buying journey.

Someone hears about your company and asks whether the business is legitimate, what the reviews are like, what the downsides are, who the competitors are and whether there is a better option.

Your potential customer may be researching you in an environment you do not control.

Your broader digital footprint matters more than ever.

Depending on the platform and query, AI systems may draw on your website, reviews, comparison pages, publications, directories, forums, news coverage and other available sources.

So there are really two sides to the problem.

First, your own website needs to clearly explain what you do, who you serve, what things cost, how you compare, what use cases you support and what results customers have achieved.

Give AI systems accurate information to work with.

But your website is not the entire internet.

The second part is what exists about you elsewhere: credible editorial coverage, relevant backlinks, reviews, third-party mentions, independent comparisons and industry references.

Those sources give AI systems additional evidence about who you are and where you fit.

That is exactly why SEO Stuff combines content and authority:

https://t.co/MMsDTFf4rg

The content builds out the questions buyers are asking, while the authority side strengthens the third-party footprint around the brand.

And this becomes especially important for non-branded questions.

There is a huge difference between:

“Is Salesforce good?”

and:

“What is the best CRM for a 15-person B2B company that needs HubSpot integration and does not want to spend more than $500 per month?”

The second question creates room for brands the buyer may never have considered.

Businesses should be answering questions like best X for Y, X vs. Y, alternatives to X, how much does X cost, is X worth it, who is X best for, what are the disadvantages and what should I look for before choosing?

There is also an important Google angle.

65.01% of AI users surveyed said they had replaced at least some product-related Google searches with AI chatbot conversations, but the study did not find that people had simply abandoned Google.

For many consumers, AI is complementing it.

That is why I do not think businesses should choose between SEO and AI Search Optimization.

You need both.
